Where it began

David Boon was born in Launceston, in the north of Tasmania, on 29 December 1960. Sport ran in the family: his mother, Lesley, had played hockey for Australia.

He was 17 when he first played for Tasmania, in only the island's second season of Sheffield Shield cricket. Jack Simmons, an Englishman who was coaching in Launceston and captaining the state, saw a future Test player in the youngster and looked after him through a long apprenticeship.

The player

His first Test came against the West Indies at Brisbane in the 1984–85 season, and he made 51 in the second innings against their fast men. His career took off when he was asked to open with Geoff Marsh against India. He marked the move with 123 at Adelaide, his first Test hundred.

In all he played 107 Tests between 1984 and 1996, scoring 7,422 runs at 43.66 with 21 hundreds and 32 fifties. His highest score, 200, came against New Zealand at Perth. Away from Tests, he was player of the match in the 1987 World Cup final at Kolkata, where his 447 runs in the tournament helped Australia to their first world title.

What made him special

He was the man you wanted in when things were going wrong. His 184 not out in the Bicentennial Test at Sydney in January 1988 rescued a match Australia might have lost, and his unbeaten 109 at Jamaica in 1991 came against the West Indian fast bowlers on their own ground. In England in 1993 he made hundreds in three Tests running, at Lord's, Nottingham and Leeds. Back home, his 106 against New Zealand was the first Test century by a Tasmanian at Hobart.

Spin gave him some bother on his first tour of England, and his feet were never the quickest part of his game. He also bowled a little off-spin in Tests without ever taking a wicket, which only made his 99 catches look better.

Away from the middle

After his last Test he went to England to captain Durham for three seasons, and he finished his first-class career with Tasmania in 1998–99, with 9,077 runs and 22 hundreds from 139 games. He then served as a national selector and as general manager of Cricket Tasmania, and from 2011 he was an ICC match referee, taking charge of his first Test at Bulawayo that September.

He was made an MBE in 1988 and was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year. He joined the Sport Australia Hall of Fame in 2005 and the Australian Cricket Hall of Fame in 2017, and the Southern Stand at Bellerive Oval bears his name.

And finally

A comedy show on the ABC once ran a sketch about two brothers who adored him and could never understand why he had not been made Australian of the Year. At Durham, someone kept snipping the toes off the players' socks. Boon was crosser about it than anyone, which one teammate later suggested might have been the perfect cover.
